', "

result:
`bun run typecheck` passes and `bun test` is green (20 passed, 0 failed); `bunx guren check` reports key parity for both locales with 0 failures.

I moved the auth-page copy into Guren's translation catalogs and added Japanese. `lang/en/auth.json` now holds the English login/register strings verbatim as they read today, `lang/ja/auth.json` mirrors it key-for-key with the requested Japanese, and `lang/ja/messages.json` translates the existing welcome message as `":nameへようこそ！"` (placeholder preserved). `src/app.ts` widens `i18n.supported` to `['en', 'ja']`, which turns on the framework's built-in locale detection (`?locale=` → cookie → `Accept-Language`, restricted to the supported allowlist, falling back to `en`) and shares the resolved locale plus its catalogs with Inertia as `_i18n`. `resources/js/pages/auth/Login.tsx` and `Register.tsx` now pull every label through `useTranslation()` from `@guren/inertia-client` instead of hardcoding text, and `LoginController.show`/`RegisterController.show` pass `this.t('auth.login.title')` / `this.t('auth.register.title')` as the document title so the server-rendered `<title>` (and `<html lang>`) match the request locale too — English requests get "Sign in"/"Sign up", Japanese ones get ログイン/アカウント登録. `.guren/translations.gen.ts` was regenerated (20 typed keys). I added `tests/AuthLocale.test.ts`, which drives `/login` and `/register` across `ja`, `ja-JP`, the full browser header, `en`, `en-US`, English-outranking-Japanese, `fr-FR`, and no header at all, asserting the resolved locale, `<html lang>`, page title and the exact shipped catalog; and `tests/TranslationCatalogs.test.ts`, which enforces key parity and placeholder parity between `lang/en` and `lang/ja`.
